terms.comment: With a dative of the person (respondē mihi) and an accusative, or ad and the accusative, for what is answered (ad ea, quae quaesīta erant, respondēbat, Cic. Phil. 1.2). To answer a letter is rescrībere.

evidence: Quint. 1.5.36: cum respōnsum ab interrogante dissentit
terms.comment: Respōnsum reddere or dare, to give an answer.

phrases.latin: huic ego «studēs?» inquam. respondit: «etiam.» «ubi?» «Mediōlānī.» «cūr nōn hīc?»
phrases.english: I asked him, “Do you go to school?” He answered, “Yes.” “Where?” “In Milan.” “Why not here?”
You answer something other than what I ask?

phrases.latin: interrogantibus libenter respondeat, nōn interrogantēs percontētur ultrō
phrases.english: let him gladly answer those who ask, and question those who do not

re-short.html: The prefix is re-, from Proto-Italic *wre, “back” (de Vaan 516, s.v. re-, red-). Lewis & Short writes rē- before sc, sp and st, and only there. Its article on the prefix gives rĕ, with a by-form rĕd-, and puts the poets’ rēdūcō, rēlātum down to “the suppression of the d”; the long mark before s and a consonant seems to rest on the same idea, as its dī-scindō from dis- does. Bennett (The Latin Language §48) rejects that lengthening for ascendō, distinguō, suspiciō as “an untenable theory of compensatory lengthening”, and Lewis’s own Elementary Latin Dictionary (1890) prints re-spondeō. Traupman writes respondēre too.
